articles.title: Trump 'stooge' trolled for wine bar work after Truth Social CEO firing
articles.description: A former GOP lawmaker who abandoned his safe House seat to go to work for President Donald Trump — only to be fired — is now running a wine bar , reports show. In a tongue-in-cheek column for the San Francisco Gate, journalist Anabel Sosa reminded readers that ex-Rep. Devin Nunes (R-CA) was once known as the president's "stooge" during his time in Congress. Jon Fleishman, former California Republican Party, openly cracked jokes about the job shift. “I don’t know what’s better preparation for opening a wine bar, serving in Congress or being a part of the Trump organization,” Fleishman said. “Either of them would wanna make me drink a lot of wine.” Nunes is serving wine in a beachfront community once known as the "Clam Capital of the World" — a plummet from his tenure as CEO of Truth Social where he made $47 million in 2024. He made headlines during the first Trump administration as a Central Valley representative accused of meddling in Trump's Russia investigation to protect the president. He also sued a parody Twitter account called " Devin Nunes' Cow" for $250 million after it called him a "treasonous cowpoke." Nunes left Congress to run Trump's social media platform and has since re-emerged as a wine investor and owner of a new tasting room in Pismo Beach called the Nunes Wine Company. During his time in Congress, Nunes became one of Trump's biggest defenders amid an investigation into whether Russia interfered with the 2016 presidential election. He faced blowback after he was accused of colluding with the White House but was eventually cleared of any wrongdoing by an ethics committee, Sosa wrote. In 2021, Nunes resigned from Congress to become CEO of Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns Truth Social. He left that position in April of this year. .

articles.title: Retail sales slump in July
articles.description: Data: Census Bureau ; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios American consumers have powered the economy forward this year. In July, they took a breather. Why it matters: While the underlying trend in consumer demand appears solid, retail sales hit an air pocket last month, suggesting a bumpier path ahead for overall growth. Combined with a weak jobs report last week and two subdued inflation readings this week, it points to the Federal Reserve having room to be patient on potential interest rate increases this fall. Driving the news: Retail sales fell 0.6% in July, the weakest performance in more than a year and well below the 0.1% gain analysts expected. Excluding gas stations and auto dealers, there was still a 0.3% decline in sales, meaning that the weakness was evident even apart from those volatile categories. Auto dealers' sales were down 2%, gasoline stations' sales fell 0.9%, and electronic and appliance store sales declined 0.5%. Of note: Some one-off shifts pulled the numbers downward. Amazon held its Prime Day discounting event earlier this year than last, helping explain a 2.2% drop in online sales. Moreover, most World Cup games took place in June, so the associated spending would have the mechanical effect of pushing retail sales upward in early summer and creating a misleading decline in July. Yes, but: The numbers were soft even accounting for those factors, giving some pause as to how robust consumer spending will be in the second half of the year. Growth in Personal Consumption Expenditures contributed a whopping 2.1 percentage points to overall GDP growth in the second quarter, even as other sectors combined to subtract from GDP. The retail sales control group that feeds directly into GDP calculations fell 0.4% in July, versus a 0.3% gain that analysts forecast, and previously reported gains for May and June were revised downward. What they're saying: "The weaker July retail sales report shows that consumers took a breather last month after an ebullient burst of spending in the first half of the year," Nationwide chief economist Kathy Bostjancic wrote in a note. "The contraction in core retail control spending last month, following downward revisions to the prior two months, translates into a bit less momentum for real consumer spending starting Q3 than previously expected." Reality check: The stock market is booming, gasoline prices are well off their recent highs, and the unemployment rate is low. There is no reason to expect broader consumer spending to experience a meaningful pullback. But the July retail numbers suggest there's no major acceleration taking place, either.
